title: The Organisation Behind the Business Case
author: Richard Claydon
summary: Richard Claydon steps back from his three AI-focused Maya stories to name the underlying organizational pattern they all shared, then uses it to introduce a new series about strategy execution. He identifies three 'architectures' each AI story exposed — of agency (who can act), of expertise (who can be trusted), and of judgement (what leaders can see) — and argues the deeper lesson has little to do with AI specifically: whenever an organization improves one part of its capacity, the surrounding system must absorb the consequences, and the resulting burden often 'travels' somewhere less visible rather than disappearing. Claydon then generalizes this to strategic priority-setting, arguing that organizations rarely suffer a shortage of good, individually justified priorities; the real difficulty is that these priorities compete for the same finite people and attention, and organizations systematically avoid the 'discipline of subtraction' needed to resolve that competition explicitly. Instead, subtraction happens invisibly — deferred improvement work, fragmented specialist attention, and unpaid overtime — producing a self-reinforcing loop in which strong headline delivery, built on hidden compensation, earns organizations 'permission to add more priorities.' The piece's sharpest reframe is treating employee 'heroics' not as evidence a system is working but as diagnostic 'data' revealing where a portfolio has quietly exceeded its real capacity, closing with the provocation that strategy is best tested not by what an organization says it wants, but by what it is willing to give up.
points: Claydon's reinforcing loop — 'more legitimate priorities → weak subtraction → accumulated commitments → hidden compensation → strong headline delivery → permission to add more priorities' — gives leaders a diagnostic model for why organizations keep adding initiatives even when everyone privately knows capacity is already exceeded.

His reframe of employee 'heroics' as diagnostic 'data' rather than proof of a well-functioning system challenges leaders to treat visible resilience and hard work as a warning signal about hidden compensation, not simply as something to celebrate.

The closing test — 'strategy becomes much more revealing when we ask what they are prepared to give up' rather than what they want — offers a concrete, portable diagnostic question for evaluating whether any organization's stated priorities are real or merely aspirational.
quotes: Over the past week, I published three stories about Maya and AI. All three stories began in roughly the same place. The technology worked. Then the work moved.

The architecture of agency: who or what can act? The architecture of expertise: who can establish whether the work deserves trust? The architecture of judgement: what can leaders see, compare and consider before they decide?
An organisation changes one part of its capacity. The surrounding architecture then has to absorb the consequences. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the burden travels.

Addition is easy to legitimise because every new demand arrives attached to a reason. Subtraction carries a different political and emotional weight. So organisations frequently avoid explicit subtraction.

More legitimate priorities → weak subtraction → accumulated commitments → hidden compensation → strong headline delivery → permission to add more priorities. There is no villain in the loop. That is part of its durability.

Repeated discretionary effort also contains information. When teams continually need to work around conflicting priorities, something is being revealed. Heroics are data. The difficult leadership move is learning to read them.
Organisations are usually quite good at describing what they want. Strategy becomes much more revealing when we ask what they are prepared to give up.
